name: Crow Creek Sioux Tribe of the Crow Creek Reservation, South Dakota
land_summary: The Crow Creek Sioux Tribe's people descend from the Mdewakantunwan and Ihanktunwanna (Hunkpatina) bands, and the tribe describes its homeland as 125,000 acres of sovereign territory held in trust along the Missouri River, mostly in Buffalo County, South Dakota. Federal history here begins in 1863, when Dakota and Ho-Chunk people exiled from Minnesota were landed at Crow Creek in a time of great hardship. The Dakota were moved to Nebraska in 1866, and Yanktonai families made the place home. The 1868 treaty with the Sioux bands recognized it as Indian land. In February 1885 an executive order opened the reservation to settlers; two months later President Grover Cleveland revoked it and ordered the newcomers to leave. The Act of March 2, 1889, fixed the reservation's boundaries township by township. In the 1950s and 1960s the Fort Randall and Big Bend dams took more than 15,000 acres of Missouri River bottomland, and in 1996 Congress created a development trust fund as added compensation.

timeline.event: Dakota and Ho-Chunk people removed from Minnesota are landed at Crow Creek in May and June.
The Santee Dakota are moved from Crow Creek to a new reservation in Nebraska.
The 1868 treaty with the Sioux bands recognizes the Crow Creek area as Indian land.
A February 27 executive order opens the Crow Creek and Old Winnebago lands to settlement; on April 17 President Grover Cleveland revokes it and orders settlers to leave within 60 days.
The Act of March 2, 1889 (Section 6) sets apart a permanent reservation for the Crow Creek Agency by township and range, and allotment follows.
Public Law 85-916 authorizes taking 9,418 acres of Crow Creek land for the Fort Randall Dam project.
Public Law 87-735 authorizes taking 6,179 acres of Crow Creek land for the Big Bend Dam project.
The Crow Creek Sioux Tribe Infrastructure Development Trust Fund Act sets up a fund of up to $27.5 million as added compensation for the dam takings.

homelands: The tribe's enrollment office describes the homeland as lying on the Missouri River, about 60 miles southeast of Pierre and 26 miles northwest of Chamberlain, mostly within Buffalo County: 125,000 acres of sovereign territory held in trust, in three districts, Big Bend (Kahmi Tanka), Crow Creek (Kangi Okute) and Fort Thompson (Cunkicakse).

notes: crowcreeksiouxtribe.com refuses automated access. The 125,000-acre trust figure is the tribe's own, from its enrollment office site. The SD Dept. of Tribal Relations repeats it. Other figures conflict: SD State Archives gives 125,591 acres, and Senate Report 104-362 gives 258,361 acres, which likely counts all land within the boundaries. Dam acreage also varies: Senate Report 104-362 gives 9,154, 9,514 or 9,418 acres for Fort Randall and 6,179 or 6,417 for Big Bend. The timeline uses the statute's figures (PL 104-223), which GAO matches. A 1987 SD Attorney General opinion argues the 1863 Act did not itself create a reservation. The 1863 entry describes the removal, not the founding of a reservation. Left out for lack of a second independent source: Drifting Goose's Hunkpati band settling at Crow Creek in 1880 and Hayes's 65,000-acre James River reservation (SD Archives only), the April 26, 1949 constitution (SD Tribal Relations only), and the flooding of the old Fort Thompson townsite (ICT only). The Crow Creek Tribal School 'Cultural History' page was read but not used: it is a retyped 1986 report with an internal date conflict.
